title: How Expedia Rigs Travel Markets and Raises Your Hotel Prices
author: Lee Hepner
content:
In three weeks, Americans are about to vote for change in a midterm election.
It will be the seventh straight election that they have done so, even though
nothing seems to make any difference. A few weeks after casting their votes,
they will experience the high costs and frustrations of travel, as they head
on Thanksgiving and then Christmas holiday. Travel isn't why people are angry,
but the cause of the anger, a rigged system reaching into our pockets
constantly and persistently, is very much on display when you get on the road.

As travel writer Christopher Elliott
[notes](https://www.usatoday.com/story/travel/columnist/2026/02/17/travel-
becoming-a-luxury-for-everyday-americans/88664655007/), it isn't just one cost
upsetting customers; it's a whole set of overlapping fees and nickel-and-
diming in the experience, the canceled flights, higher gas prices, and bank-
busting hotel prices. Lodging is particularly bad, he argues, showing a "surge
in average U.S. hotel rates, from $103 a night in 2020 to $162 a night in
2025, an increase of almost 58%."

Most discussions about travel costs by the media frame the cause as high
demand, oil prices, or too much consumer spending. Americans just want to see
each other, and alas, that's costly. But I'm going to explain why they are
wrong, and what we're dealing with is an obvious conspiracy. It's called
Expedia, and it is responsible for 80% of every dollar spent booking hotels on
the internet. And for a frame of reference, on its last investor call, the
company
[noted](https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-2026-Earnings-
Presentation-Final.pdf) that price per hotel booking increased by 5% over the
last year, which is twice the rate of inflation.

Now, Expedia is not the _only_ conspiracy at work here. There are others, such
as hotel consolidation, junk fees, and hidden pricing algorithms. But what
Expedia is doing is worth highlighting, because it plays a sort of ringmaster
role in setting prices in the hotel space, not just for people who use
Expedia, but even for those who don't. The story is explained in a new lawsuit
alleging a price fixing conspiracy engineered by the firm.

Here's how it works.

Expedia has power because of its huge share of online bookings. If you are a
hotel, you must list on the site, or you can't get customers. The
[lawsuit](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601/gov.uscourts.wawd.369601.1.0.pdf)
alleges that Expedia Group, which also owns Hotels.com, Travelocity, and
Orbitz, leverages its status as a critical channel for booking to charge
hotels commissions anywhere from 15% to 30%. Indeed, the company's executives
bragged to investors in August about this pricing power, chalking up increased
profit margins to "our supplier-funded promotions," which are the kickbacks
that hotels offer the middleman.

But there's an important second layer to the problem. Those commissions get
baked into hotel prices not just on Expedia but on direct bookings with hotels
and other online travel agencies, like Booking.com, which also owns Priceline,
Kayak, and Agoda. It even gets baked into higher prices for most hotels on
their own websites.

According to the lawsuit, hotels listed on Expedia are subject to what's
called a most-favored-nation clause. An MFN is a contract that says they have
to give Expedia their best price, and they can't offer a lower price anywhere
else. That's why when you go to a hotel website, it's rarely lower than
Expedia, even though it's buying direct. Now, this dynamic wouldn't be a
problem if Expedia didn't charge high fees. But it does. So if a hotel raises
their prices on Expedia to recover Expedia's 15-30% commission on each
booking, they can't also charge a lower price on their own website or on other
booking channels that don't charge that 15-30% commission. The commission is
baked into every distribution channel.

There's an enforcement mechanism for hotels who disobey. According to the
suit, Expedia suppresses hotels in Expedia's search results when hotels offer
lower prices on their own websites or in other channels. If a hotel performs
poorly on "rate competitiveness" - which is not at all about price competition
but rather about ensuring that Expedia's listings reflect the lowest price in
the market - its listings are demoted in search results.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BN-Q!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F17008458-aaa8-4728-a16f-630d31c2b62c_1062x373.png)

Expedia enforces its most-favored-nation clause, or lowest-price mandate, by
suppressing hotels who perform poorly on "rate competitiveness."

To state the obvious, being listed higher in search results is critical for
increasing hotel bookings. Expedia itself
[advises](https://partner.expediagroup.com/en-us/resources/blog/travel-
marketplace-visibility-guide) properties that appear in the top 10 of search
results receive 62% of clicks.

Expedia also has an "automatic rate match" tool that alerts hotels when they
offer lower rates outside of Expedia and automatically lowers rates on Expedia
to match the "best available rate." The automatic rate matching tool further
suppresses competition with non-Expedia booking sites, and is a self-executing
mechanism that hotels are coerced into using.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a-rW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c176919-fba4-4f7c-885d-69f5b7a08484_658x598.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a-rW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2c176919-fba4-4f7c-885d-69f5b7a08484_658x598.png)Expedia
encourages hotels to use its automatic rate match tool, which enforces its
lowest price guarantee.

Finally, Expedia offers a VIP Access program that gives hotels access to
Expedia-operated marketing campaigns and results in 42% higher bookings than
non-VIP listings. In order to be eligible for the VIP Access program, hotels
are required to price rooms 10-25% _higher_ on non-Expedia channels
indefinitely. So the VIP Access program isn't just about rate parity with
other booking channels. It kills nascent competition, and it serves as a _de
facto_ rate inflation scheme for all listings outside of Expedia.

There's a silver lining here, though not for you and me. The high prices we
pay for travel are mirrored in the high profits to Expedia, whose stock is up
by 65% since the war in Iran started last April. Their CEO, Ariane Gorin, just
can't help but
[brag](https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/EXPE-
USQ_Transcript_2026-08-05.pdf) to investors about the [higher margins from
higher
prices](https://s202.q4cdn.com/757635260/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Q2-2026-Earnings-
Presentation-Final.pdf). That's almost certainly not flowing back to the
hotels themselves, as Gorin pointed out the company's margin increase is
coming from the hotels who pay for advertising to access Expedia customers.

In August, Matt [wrote](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-
time-bandits-and) about how Expedia cheats both customers and hotels, and its
contract is so strict that the hotel owner wasn't even allowed to show the fee
he had to pay the online booking middleman:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!o8CU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F22ad1727-a4a2-4e1e-a8d2-6c642c06baa6_636x912.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!o8CU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F22ad1727-a4a2-4e1e-a8d2-6c642c06baa6_636x912.png)An
itemized receipt for a hotel booking redacts key information, including the
"Amount Retained by Expedia Group."

The new lawsuit just adds some texture. Now, I
[posted](https://x.com/LeeHepner/status/2109709285748039991?s=20) about this
scheme on social media a couple of days ago, and a lot of people have
responded that this is why they don't use Expedia, or are incredulous that
anyone still does (they quantifiably _do_.) Others have encouraged an Expedia
boycott. But these responses miss the central point of the alleged Expedia
scheme: You are paying higher hotel prices whether you book on Expedia or not.
Expedia's restraints inflate hotel prices on the hotel's own booking channel
and on all other online travel agencies. You can't simply avoid higher prices
on Expedia by booking elsewhere, because Expedia's commissions and most-
favored-nation provisions permeate every other booking channel, too.

### It's Not Just Hotels, It's Everything

The allegations against Expedia have also elicited frustration that the entire
economy seems to be rigged. Not only is this observation correct, but many
markets are rigged in exactly the same way that Expedia allegedly rigs hotel
prices.

The clearest analog are the
[allegations](https://www.economicliberties.us/california-v-amazon/)
[against](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-
proceedings/1910129-1910130-amazoncom-inc-amazon-ecommerce) Amazon, now
pending in major lawsuits by the Federal Trade Commission and the State of
California, which allege Amazon is hiking prices across the retail economy
through a coercive price parity scheme that looks strikingly similar to
Expedia's. Amazon too, punishes third party sellers on its platform by
eliminating the coveted "Buy Box" from product listings when those sellers
offer lower prices on non-Amazon channels. Removing the Buy Box can decimate a
seller's whole business, much like how Expedia has become a critical booking
channel for hotels. So, while Amazon holds itself out as the place to find
lowest price details, those prices are only low relative to the higher prices
coerced by Amazon.

Other parallels can be observed in online food delivery platforms like Uber
Eats and DoorDash, which, along with Postmates (acquired by Uber Eats in 2020)
and Caviar (acquired by DoorDash in 2019), faced restaurant industry blowback
and [regulatory
scrutiny](https://www.sfchronicle.com/food/restaurants/article/Food-app-
delivery-commission-in-S-F-capped-at-16266468.php) in 2019 even before
shelter-in-place orders decimated in-restaurant dining and made online food
delivery services all-but essential. A big part of that controversy was about
food delivery platforms charging 30% commissions to restaurants listed on
their platforms (often without their
[consent](https://www.foxbusiness.com/small-business/doordash-grubhub-
restaurant-listing-without-permission)), while restricting restaurants from
offering cheaper menu prices for dining in. (A feather in my cap, several
years ago now I wrote the first municipal
[law](https://www.sfchronicle.com/food/restaurants/article/Food-app-delivery-
commission-in-S-F-capped-at-16266468.php) capping predatory restaurant
commissions and liberating restaurants from margin-destroying price parity
clauses.) Similar to the allegations against Expedia, that 30% commission
risked being priced into menu items even for non-delivery dining, or else
restaurants, with their notoriously thin margins, had to figure out how else
to eat the added costs.

There's also an important consolidation story here. As mentioned above,
Expedia Group also owns Hotels.com, Travelocity, and Orbitz, all of which were
acquired by Expedia in 2015. Booking Holdings, formerly Priceline Group, has
an eye-popping string of multi-billion dollar acquisitions stretching back two
decades, and now owns Priceline, Booking.com, Kayak, and Agoda. Booking
Holdings expanded beyond hotels when it acquired OpenTable in 2014 for $2.6
billion, which isn't exactly relevant to hotel bookings, but is nevertheless a
shocking data point in the empire-by-acquisition story.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Y66!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b5f234c-a3a1-43b4-afe4-39b27b2f5179_497x332.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6Y66!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b5f234c-a3a1-43b4-afe4-39b27b2f5179_497x332.png)Expedia
Group and Booking Holdings control dozens of online travel agency portals.

So, to the extent you'd expect more competition on all of these online travel
agencies, even without Expedia's alleged pricing restraints you're actually
seeing very little. That's bad for hotels seeking better commission structures
and, ultimately, for travelers who end up absorbing higher hotel prices.

If all of this is true, the "lowest price," whether on Amazon or Expedia, is a
mask for economy-wide market-rigging schemes that actually bake monopoly
commissions and other fees into the prices of goods and services, while
preventing the very price competition that would lower prices further. If
Expedia is the lowest price platform, it's only because they prohibit hotels
from offering their prices at lower rates anywhere else.

To turn a phrase, one might call it "artificial inflation," and Expedia's
alleged conduct is only one piece of the puzzle.

### A Multi-Level Enshittification Scheme: Consolidation, Price Fixing, and
Deception

The infrastructure of our economy is rigged, and even though the allegations
against Expedia implicate potential 30% price hikes across the board, it would
be too convenient to lay all of the frustration at Expedia's feet. More
accurate would be to situate the allegations against Expedia in a decades-long
multi-layered scheme to maximize profits, cut competition, and push the
boundaries of consumer willingness to pay.

The longest-running gambit is the trend toward consolidation across the hotel
industry. Hotel markets are geographically localized, which makes sense
inasmuch as the level of industry concentration in a place like New York City
has little to say about the number of competitors in Detroit. Markets have
also become more segmented in the past half century, with different classes of
hotels catering to, say, business travelers with limited needs, as opposed to
more full-service hotel suites. With those significant caveats aside, the
consolidation of brands under just a few hotel groups is startling.

Marriott's $13.6 billion acquisition of Starwood Hotels in 2016 made it the
largest hotel company in the world, with 30 brands (since
[expanded](https://frugalflyer.ca/blog/marriott-hotel-brands-explained/) to 39
brands) spanning luxury offerings to more affordable "select" options. In
February 2016, the FTC and DOJ cleared the acquisition, which was the largest
hotel merger in decades, consolidating 1.1 million hotel rooms across 110
countries, without so much as a [second request](https://www.ftc.gov/advice-
guidance/competition-guidance/guide-antitrust-laws/mergers/premerger-
notification-merger-review-process) regarding potential anti-competitive
effects:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!edqE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0db24852-9537-4e9a-a09d-5f76f60b7af4_962x628.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!edqE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0db24852-9537-4e9a-a09d-5f76f60b7af4_962x628.png)The
2016 merger of Marriott and Starwood was one of the largest hotel acquisitions
in history, combining 30 brands under one corporate umbrella.

Today, just three brands -- Hilton, Marriott, and Choice International -
[represent](https://www.scrapehero.com/location-reports/10-largest-hotels-in-
the-usa/) 56% of the top 10 hotel brands in the country, by number of
locations, and the array of brands under each hotel group lends to a false
impression of competition. Competition _between_ hotel groups, or _inter_
-brand competition, is softened by two other features of the hotel industry:
First, loyalty programs that encourage [brand
loyalty](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10963480251352229) at the
hotel group level and reduce the likelihood that participants will interact
with different hotel groups as actual competitors for their patronage. And
second, [non-exclusive](https://www.ftc.gov/reports/branding-cannibalization-
spatial-preemption-application-hotel-industry) franchisor-franchisee
relationships, which can lead to a single franchisee controlling pricing and
other competitive decisions across different hotel brands in the same area.

Ultimately, decades of concentration and the spawning of new hotel brands --
often with the purpose of cutting off independent entrants -- betrays what the
naked eye might otherwise perceive as robust competition.

Another layer of enshittification is an alleged algorithmic price fixing
scheme that spans every major hotel group in the country. In recent years,
multiple lawsuits have exposed the scourge of algorithmic market rigging among
hotels. Among the largest is a
[lawsuit](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.441223/gov.uscourts.cand.441223.1.0.pdf)
against virtually every major hotel chain and a company called SAS Institute,
a business analytics firm that offers AI-based pricing "solutions," including
the G3 Revenue Management System. The extensive complaint sheds light on how
decision making algorithms are automating price decisions that "drive
incremental revenue," aka price increases. An interesting wrinkle in all of
this is that hotel chains are also chasing upstream financial investment,
including by private equity firms, so participation in a data-sharing and
price optimization scheme becomes yet another variable for survival.

Other cases, like _Gibson v. Cendyn_ and _Cornish-Adebiyi v. Caesars,_ have
gone after more localized algorithmic price fixing schemes in high-propensity
tourist markets, like the Las Vegas Strip and Atlantic City. I wrote about
Cendyn's algorithmic pricing tool, hilariously called "Rainmaker," for BIG a
few years ago in a piece called "The Banality of Price Fixing." Both the
_Gibson_ and _Cornish-Adebiyi_ cases allege that participating hotels used the
same algorithmic pricing services to automatically accept recommended prices
90% of the time, meaning individual hotels had basically delegated their core
pricing decisions to the same third party. But only the case against _Caesars_
has been allowed to proceed, while the 9th Circuit dismissed the _Gibson_ case
without allowing plaintiffs to uncover the details of how the Rainmaker
algorithm functioned _._

The collapse of the _Gibson_ case is not necessarily attributable to it being
a weaker case on the merits, but because 20 years ago, the Supreme Court, in a
case called _[Twombly](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/550/544/),
_granted corporations another shield, in the form of a new mandate for judges
to kick cases out of court based on limited available facts. Even the "Dean of
the Antitrust Bar" Herb Hovenkamp, who is notoriously antagonistic to Neo-
Brandesians, and whose treatise -- it should be noted -- is quoted throughout
the _Twombly_ opinion, is scrambling to make sense of the consequent
proliferation of "[cartel management
services](https://download.ssrn.com/2026/9/1/6318841.pdf?response-content-
disposition=inline&X-Amz-Security-

I'll ask you to excuse this brief legal rant with the following takeaway:
Price fixing has always been patently illegal, at least in principle, but
today, price fixing conspiracies are concealed in code, which makes them
harder to detect and harder to prevent. The age of illegal business dealings
in smoky back rooms has been replaced by the proliferation of far more
efficient and widespread algorithmic cartels. And while Congress could easily
[fix this](https://scanlon.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=2011)
and kill a lot of illegal cartels in their cradle, doing so would make a lot
of private equity firms mad.

On top of the consolidation and optimized price fixing is a final layer of
enshittification, which is the retail deception that too many people in
America are intimately familiar with. This is where you find pricing scams
like "junk fees," which conceal the all-in price of hotel rooms with
miscellaneous, unavoidable charges added at checkout. This is the "resort
fee," or the "booking fee," or any other number of inexplicable charges tacked
onto the advertised price of a hotel room.

There's been good progress at the policy level to address junk fees, including
a rule banning junk fees under Lina Khan's FTC, but compliance is another
issue. For example, I was recently headed to DC on a work trip and quickly
snagged a room at one of my favorite hotels when I saw a pretty good deal on
third-party booking site Agoda. But when it came time to check in, the hotel
hit me with a $40 per night resort fee -- more than 15% of the reservation
price. Now, my modus operandi here is never to be _rude_ to a customer service
representative, they aren't punching bags for bad decisions made in
boardrooms, but I did ask about it. And, lo and behold, in the small print of
the Agoda reservation was a disclosure that I'd be charged a resort fee at the
property itself.

It's a classic case of deception, inducing consumers to purchase at what
appears to be a good deal, only to tack on unavoidable, hidden fees that erase
the deal entirely. In my case, the property absolved itself of responsibility.

### The Affordability Crisis is a Rule of Law Crisis

It brings me no joy to write another story about how everything is bad and
this is why we can't have good things. So let's be clear: The case against
Expedia is good news. The pending cases against the major hotel chains for
forming nationwide and local cartels to fix hotel rates is also good news. The
fact that a wave of lawmakers is taking it upon themselves to pass new laws
reinforcing consumer protection laws against junk fees, and making it easier
to bring price fixing cases in the first instance is GOOD news.

If antitrust laws can be successfully enforced -- a prospect made more
difficult by a string of Supreme Court decisions dating back a couple of
decades, principally _Twombly_ and _Leegin_ -- maybe we _can_ have good
things. That looks like forcing prices to be set competitively, liberated from
the restraints of central coordinating platforms or coercive third-party
pricing services. That means a return to the "heads in beds" strategy of
setting hotel prices, where the imperative is to maximize bookings, even if
that means offering a lower-than-"optimal" price that only seeks to maximize
revenue. Unrigging the market will also lend to a greater likelihood of
independent market entry, because rigged markets constrain the beneficial
risk-taking necessary to align financial investment with innovative business
propositions. And so on.

And it's all possible if we demand a populist reorientation of our politics
that is laser-focused on holding the powerful accountable. An antitrust and
consumer protection movement with actual teeth:

As Americans head to the polls in a few weeks, and then head to family dinners
to argue with each other about their chosen candidates, it's worth keeping the
Expedia story in mind. The reason is that Americans of all political
persuasions are united against this kind of corrupt and extractive behavior.
The only question is how to get the people we elect to do something about it.

_The lawsuit discussed above is_ Andrews v. Expedia Group, Inc., _Case No.
2:26-cv-03743 (W.D. Wash.). The full docket can be
found[here](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/74912898/andrews-v-expedia-
group-inc/)._
